newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia debt payment default delays World Bank projects.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia debt payment default delays World Bank projects.

text.p: The World Bank said on Monday that loans and new reconstruction projects for Bosnia-Herzegovina were suspended after the country failed to make an $8 million payment on its external debt.
Bosnia's inter-ethnic government failed to pay the installment within a 30-month grace period which expired last Friday, Patrice Dufour, spokesman for the World Bank's office in Sarajevo, said.
The default meant that World Bank approval for four peacetime reconstruction projects would be delayed until the debt was resolved, Dufour told Reuters.
"We are now not allowed to present new projects to our board of directors, which means four projects now in the pipeline cannot be processed," Dufour said.
The World Bank projects included funds for transport, school textbooks, repairs to schools and a reconstruction programme for the country's Serb entity, he said.
Bosnia owes two billion dollars as its share of former Yugoslavia's debt and is currently servicing a consolidated $680 million loan to the World Bank with regular six-month payments.
Officials from the country's cash-strapped Serb entity say they have no funds to pay their $3.8 million share of the $8 million instalment.
A 1995 peace treaty divides Bosnia into autonomous entities, the Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation, which are supposed to be governed by a small central government.
The Serb entity's economy is lagging behind the federation and is already in arrears for unpaid pensions and wages to public employees.

The Bosnian Serb republic received only about two percent of more than a billion dollars in international aid which poured into the country last year because Serb authorities have failed to abide by terms of a peace agreement.

If the debt is not paid within 45 days, Bosnia could also be deprived of World Bank replenishment for liquidity accounts and risks suspension of all disbursements for ongoing reconstruction projects after 60 days of non-payment.

The World Bank said it hopes the debt will be resolved before an international fund-raising conference for Bosnia scheduled for June 24 in Brussels. Officials are concerned that the debt problem could undermine plans to win pledges for an estimated $1.4 billion in post-war aid.

As one of the sponsors of the donors' conference, the default put the World Bank in an awkward position, Dufour said. "The donors will say you are asking us for money and they are not even paying you," he said.
